title: Inside the fish (Jonah 2)
hook: three days in the dark, Jonah prays from the belly

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonah runs: a ticket west, a storm, a prophet asleep in the hold. Your line was you can't outrun him. Did you take one small step toward the thing you've been avoiding? Day four hundred eighty-six.

The sailors let go of him, and the sea closes over his head. Seaweed. Cold. The last light going green, then gone. And then, in the King James Bible, one of the strangest sentences in scripture: "Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah." Notice the word prepared. The fish isn't an accident or a punishment out of nowhere. It was ready. And then the story does something you might not expect. It doesn't describe the inside of the fish at all. No ribs, no stomach, no smell. It skips straight to what Jonah does in there.

He prays. Chapter two says: "Then Jonah prayed unto the LORD his God out of the fish's belly." Up to now, Jonah has done everything except pray. He slept while pagan sailors prayed. The captain had to shake him awake. Now, at the very bottom, three days and three nights in the dark, the words finally come. And the prayer is a surprise. It's shaped like a psalm, and many of its lines echo the Psalms, as if Jonah reached for the prayers he'd known since childhood. He describes drowning: the waters closing in, weeds wrapped around his head, going down to the roots of the mountains. And he says: "out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice." Hell there is the old English for Sheol, the place of the dead. He feels as far from God as a person can get. Here's what's strange: the prayer is mostly thanks. He thanks God for hearing him while he's still inside the fish, before anything has changed. It ends with a short line, "Salvation is of the LORD." Then the fish spits him out onto dry land. And one more thing. The Bible never calls it a whale. The Hebrew says a great fish. The whale came later, in some translations of Jesus's words in Matthew, where he points to Jonah's three days in the dark as a sign of his own three days in the grave. Christians have heard Jonah's prayer as Easter in miniature ever since: someone given up for lost, praying from the bottom, and brought back up.
screen: `A PSALM FROM THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA.`
then, large: `SALVATION IS OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray from wherever you are. Settle, and breathe. Jonah didn't wait to be out of the fish. He didn't tidy up first. He prayed from the dark, in the mess, with weeds around his head. So, wherever you are right now, on a bus, in bed, in a hard week, notice what it actually feels like down here. Name it plainly. Then, if you can, find one thing to be grateful for, even before anything changes. If you pray, you can speak to God from exactly this spot. If you don't, simply say the honest words to yourself and let them be heard. The bell holds the time.
Inside the fish. Three days and three nights in the dark, where Jonah, who wouldn't pray on the ship, finally prays, and gives thanks before he's out.
Your line: prayer from the belly. Today, when you hit a low moment, don't wait to feel better first. Speak from right there, honestly, and see what changes. Day four hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Christians often read Jonah 2 alongside Jesus's words about the sign of Jonah in Matthew 12, and Jonah's escape from the fish appears in very early Christian art, including catacomb paintings, as a picture of resurrection.

original.note: Hebrew: a great fish. the book never says whale.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a man surviving inside a whale.
what it means: the prophet who wouldn't pray finally prays from the very bottom, and gives thanks before he's rescued.
what a scholar hears: Jonah's prayer is built like a psalm and echoes lines from the Psalms, and Jesus names the sign of Jonah in Matthew 12.

notes: Jonah 1:17 is numbered 2:1 in Hebrew Bibles. Confirm citation convention.
'Hell' in Jonah 2:2 KJV renders Sheol. Confirm.
The prayer's echoes of the Psalms (e.g. Psalm 42:7, 18, 120:1): stated generally. Confirm.
The KJV of Matthew 12:40 says 'whale' (Greek ketos, a sea creature); stated as 'some translations of Jesus's words in Matthew'. Confirm.
Jonah imagery in early Christian catacomb art (howItsDone): widely documented; confirm phrasing.
